title: Style Guide vs Brand Guide: Which One Does Your Business Need?
author: Alyona Deieieva
excerpt: A recent [Storyblok survey](https://www.storyblok.com/mp/inconsistent-brands) found that 73% of shoppers are less likely to buy from a brand that feels inconsistent. Yet ask ten agencies what separates a style guide from a brand guide, and

body.text: A recent [Storyblok survey](https://www.storyblok.com/mp/inconsistent-brands) found that 73% of shoppers are less likely to buy from a brand that feels inconsistent. Yet ask ten agencies what separates a style guide from a brand guide, and you'll get ten different answers. And this confusion may cost founders a lot of time and money. Teams brief the wrong document, and all brand elements may ship inconsistently across different channels.

Arounda studied 15 public brand documents to map what style guide vs brand guide means. This guide breaks down the real difference, when you need one document or both, and a brief template you can hand to any design company.
Article Key Takeaways

items: Style guides set the rules for voice, tone, and editorial standards and keep all written communication consistent.
Brand guides are more about the visual identity because they lock down logos, color values, typography, and design assets.
Arounda analyzed 15 public documents from companies like Apple, Slack, Adobe, and Mailchimp to highlight what industry leaders get right and where most guides fall short.

Our experts break down the design framework for [fintech](/industries/fintech), [Web3](/industries/web3), [AI](/industries/ai), and [cybersecurity](/industries/cybersecurity) brands, complete with expert commentary, a brief template, and strategies for managing complex corporations with subsidiaries.

body.text: We Looked at 15 Public Brand Documents. Here's What We Found

Companies name these documents differently, and what's inside them differs even more. Before you build your own brand identity guidelines, it helps to see what well-known companies got right and wrong. Here's what we found.
Mailchimp

body.alt: Online style guide for Mailchimp detailing voice pillars and visual assets
body.caption: Online style guide for Mailchimp detailing voice pillars and visual assets

body.text: This company has a one-page brand book which includes logo spacing, mascot rules, and two brand colors. It reads more like a quick reference card than a document a design team would build a system around.
Gaps:

items: Doesn't include typography guidance anywhere on the page
Voice and tone live in a separate document most visitors never find
The do/don't list is text only, no side-by-side example of correct vs incorrect use

body.text: The best thing is the FAQ section, as it answers all questions beginners typically have.
**Arounda suggests:** Connect visual rules and writing standards inside a single portal so your team can verify brand details without hunting across different documents.
Buffer

body.alt: Buffer brand guidelines page presenting social media visual standards and logo assets
body.caption: Buffer brand guidelines page presenting social media visual standards and logo assets

body.text: Buffer has a style guide which is built around voice and doesn't include visual content.
Gaps:

items: No logo, color, or typography reference anywhere in the document
Lives in a shared doc rather than a stable page, so old bookmarks can break
No link back to a visual identity document, if one exists

body.text: One line does more work than most full pages elsewhere: "you have the same voice all the time, but your tone changes." That distinction alone would improve half the documents on this list.
**Arounda suggests:** We recommend adding or linking to visual assets (even if it is a lightweight style guide).
Slack

body.alt: Page from Slack brand manual demonstrating co-branding lockups and logo padding
body.caption: Page from Slack brand manual demonstrating co-branding lockups and logo padding

body.text: A 40+ page PDF covering mission, values, voice, and full visual identity in one file. Logo, color, and two named typefaces (Larsseit, Slack Circular) sit next to voice and tone, so nobody has to check two places for basic answers.
Gaps:

items: No table of contents links or searchable index inside the PDF
Five named values (empathy, courtesy, craftsmanship, playfulness, solidarity) include definitions, but there are no examples
It is too long. A new hire is unlikely to read 40 pages before shipping a first deliverable

body.text: **Arounda suggests:** When working on long brand documents, put a 2-page cheat sheet on the first slide. New hires won't need to review 50 pages before they start working.
Apple

body.alt: Apple trademark and brand guideline sheet displaying compliance rules
body.caption: Apple trademark and brand guideline sheet displaying compliance rules

body.text: A 475-page editorial dictionary, kept entirely separate from visual identity. Look up "FaceTime," get one clear rule: don't use it as a verb. That entry format is fast for daily use, which is likely why writers keep coming back.
Gaps:

items: New hires get no starting point (only an alphabetical list to search)
No tone guidance anywhere
Visual identity is in a separate PDF for resellers

body.text: **Arounda suggests:** Add a short "how to use this guide" page for new hires.
Adobe

body.alt: Developer branding page from Adobe showing logo spacing and partner guidelines
body.caption: Developer branding page from Adobe showing logo spacing and partner guidelines

body.text: This brand guide (as Adobe calls it) looks more like a trademark license for outside developers. Unfortunately, it doesn't include voice or tone (only badges and logos).
Gaps:

items: No help for anyone writing a blog post or a pitch deck
Scope stays narrow on purpose: logos, names, approved badges only

body.text: The best part is that this guide doesn't overpromise. Any developer can open it and quickly find what they can and can't use.
**Arounda suggests:** Always create separate guides for external developers. This will help keep legal conditions clear without slowing down your marketing team.
Atlassian

body.alt: Atlassian design system guide illustrating typography hierarchy and brand identity elements
body.caption: Atlassian design system guide illustrating typography hierarchy and brand identity elements

body.text: This document sets rules for Marketplace partners building apps on Jira and Confluence, but it looks like a legal checklist.
Gaps:

items: Only logo restrictions, nothing on visual identity itself
App naming rules feel like a compliance form to fill out
Doesn't include information for writing about this product

body.text: Atlassian shows an approved sentence right next to a rejected one. You see the difference instead of reading about it.
**Arounda suggests:** Other companies should do the same. A rule written down as text gets ignored. A rule shown as two examples side by side gets remembered.
Asana

body.alt: Asana brand book breakdown featuring core color codes
body.caption: Asana brand book breakdown featuring core color codes

body.text: A logo kit built around one clever rule: partner logo spacing equals the width of Asana's three-dot symbol.
Gaps:

items: Covers logo and color only, nothing on voice
Trademark legal text is in the same scroll as the visual guide
No typography guidance

body.text: Do/don't visuals are specific: six mistakes, six images, zero ambiguity.
**Arounda suggests:** Move legal trademark language to a separate linked document.
Notion

body.alt: Notion style guide layout highlighting monochrome logo rules and typography
body.caption: Notion style guide layout highlighting monochrome logo rules and typography

body.text: Notion built one hub with eight sections. One of them, Music, covers sound branding, something almost none of the other 14 documents mention.
Gaps:

items: Needs JavaScript to load (invisible without it)
Broad structure, but depth per section unclear from outside
No table of contents before diving in

body.text: Voice & Tone is next to Key Messaging, so nobody needs to check two places for one answer.
**Arounda suggests:** Place core messaging pillars on the same screen as your tone of voice rules so creators see both what to write and how to say it.
Cloudflare

body.alt: Cloudflare online brand hub with official logo lockups and vector assets
body.caption: Cloudflare online brand hub with official logo lockups and vector assets

body.text: Cloudflare split its brand hub into seven pages, one for each topic: strategy, logo, color, design elements, typography, illustration, photography.
Gaps:

items: Only one brand color named (no secondary or accent palette)
There's no typography section at all
No section about tone or voice

body.text: They state where each logo version belongs, like using icon marks for app buttons and monochrome versions over photo backgrounds.
**Arounda suggests:** Organize design standards under one main landing page, and your partners will be able to grasp your entire system in a single view.
Chatwoot

body.alt: Chatwoot open source brand identity page showing logo variations
body.caption: Chatwoot open source brand identity page showing logo variations

body.text: A single page: five logo variants, one brand color, and a short do/don't list.
Gaps:

items: Only one brand color named, no secondary or accent palette
No typography section
No voice or tone guidance

body.text: Naming the exact use case for each logo variant (icon mark for app icons, monochrome for photo backgrounds) removes guesswork.
**Arounda suggests:** Add at least two accent colors. One color forces every future asset into the same visual note.
Zendesk

body.alt: Figma presentation deck featuring Zendesk creative guidelines and Z mark rules
body.caption: Figma presentation deck featuring Zendesk creative guidelines and Z mark rules

body.text: Zendesk organizes its brand guidelines inside a public Figma deck by logo type, covering the primary logo, wordmark, and the Z symbol.
Gaps:

items: The Z symbol needs creative team approval to use alone, but the document never says how to request it
Named colors like Licorice and Coconut show no hex codes anywhere
Opening a full Figma file takes extra loading time for non-designers who just need a fast answer

body.text: Co-branding diagrams show exact clear space next to a partner logo, and publishing inside Figma lets designers copy vector assets straight into active files.
**Arounda suggests:** Show the hex code alongside color names, and publish a lightweight web summary for non-design partners.
Wero

body.alt: Overview of Wero digital wallet identity portal with logo rules and color swatches
body.caption: Overview of Wero digital wallet identity portal with logo rules and color swatches

body.text: Wero provides a brand guide covering logo usage, color palettes, pixel-grid iconography, and checkout placement rules.
Gaps:

items: Covers visual assets and payment UI without voice rules
Requires manual brand team approval before using illustrations
Places legal disclaimers on opening pages before core design rules

body.text: It includes exact 24px grid alignment, stroke widths, and color tint tables for UI icons.
**Arounda suggests:** Combine visual rules and writing guidance into one main portal.
PayPal

body.alt: PDF page from PayPal brand manual outlining logo clear space and tone rules
body.caption: PDF page from PayPal brand manual outlining logo clear space and tone rules

body.text: PayPal provides a 40-page corporate brand manual covering its logo standards, color system, typography, and verbal voice.
Gaps:

items: Locks typography to a single font weight without specifying digital or web fallback fonts
Splits merchant checkout buttons and co-branding rules into separate sub-documents
Prioritizes print layouts over modern digital interfaces

body.text: The guide offers writing rules and visual assets in one document. Plus, it asks all creators to use clear human language and avoid technical jargon.
**Arounda suggests:** Build one web portal for all brand rules instead of scattering files across multiple PDFs. This prevents costly fixes when materials go into production.
OpenAI

body.alt: OpenAI corporate identity document explaining logo geometry and margin requirements
body.caption: OpenAI corporate identity document explaining logo geometry and margin requirements

body.text: OpenAI publishes a brand guide covering logo construction, color rules, typography, and company values.
Gaps:

items: Restricts main colors to black and white with almost no secondary palette options
Omits copywriting examples and specific voice guidance for content creators
Explains logo safety margins but ignores digital product components

body.text: It sets exact minimum pixel dimensions for digital logos and requires left-aligned layouts.
**Arounda suggests:** Add UI component rules next to logo specifications so product designers do not have to guess layout spacing.
HIMSS

body.alt: Healthcare brand standards slide from HIMSS illustrating official color palette
body.caption: Healthcare brand standards slide from HIMSS illustrating official color palette

body.text: This company offers a detailed healthcare brand manual, which includes organizational mission, logo usage, color palettes, and global guidelines.
Gaps:

items: Fills early pages with corporate vision statements before showing actual design assets
You won't find downloadable assets that can be useful for developers
Prioritizes print publications over interactive web components

body.text: Defines specific audience groups across healthcare sectors. This information helps writers change the tone of voice properly.
**Arounda suggests:** Turn static PDF manuals into an online portal with downloadable design tokens for product teams.
Why the Terminology Is So Inconsistent

There's no industry group responsible for regulating these terms, so this means that anyone can name a document whatever fits their process. Different teams built the vocabulary from different starting points, which is why the brand guidelines vs style guide question keeps coming up.
What Needs to Be in the Document, Whatever You Call It
Ask what is included in a style guide, and the honest answer is: it depends on who built it. But across the 15 documents we reviewed, two categories always show up somewhere.
The Visual Rules Every Document Needs
While every company builds its documentation differently, a solid visual foundation always relies on five core components.

items: Logo specs covering primary and secondary variants, clear space rules, and minimum sizes
Color palettes (they must be documented with exact HEX, RGB, and CMYK values)
Typography rules (headline and body fonts, weights, line heights, and hierarchy)
Do and don't visual examples that show correct and incorrect usage
Clear layout rules for fitting your brand assets onto web screens, social media feeds, and physical print

body.text: To give you more specifics, here is how this looks in practice. In our [Tunnelo case study](/works/tunnelo), we prepared a complete visual guide outlining a hexagonal mark, neon-green accent palette, and pixel-inspired typeface across app UI, social templates, and print assets. For their team, the real value was speed and clarity; having clear rules reduced creative approval time by 39% because designers don’t need to spend time guessing which logo version or shade of green was correct.

body.alt: Arounda portfolio page for Tunnelo VPN brand identity
body.caption: Arounda portfolio page for Tunnelo VPN brand identity

body.text: The Strategic Rules Every Document Needs

Visual rules demonstrate how a brand looks and strategic rules explain the reasoning behind those choices. A solid document relies on four strategic elements to keep design work aligned with business goals.

items: Audience profiles that define who you speak to and how you stand out
Competitor breakdowns that help you avoid visual clichés
Tone of voice rules, as their main goal is to keep your messaging consistent across all channels
Layout standards as they connect digital screens with your print materials

body.text: For instance, in our[Loca Travel project](/works/loca-travel), we defined visual standards that cover mobile screens, social campaigns, and outdoor billboards. We know that we must align physical posters with the in-app experience, as this builds instant brand recognition and prevents trust loss between channels. This strategic approach improved brand recall by 60% and tripled marketing asset production speed.

body.alt: Loca Travel platform logo and marketing design
body.caption: Loca Travel platform logo and marketing design

body.text: "Clients come to us with a specific visual in mind. We always start by listening, but then we research the market, competitors, and brand history. Very often, after seeing data, concepts, and testing results, clients completely rethink their original ideas. Branding is a strategic process, and it shapes how people perceive you. Documenting those rules is what keeps your logo and assets identical on a phone screen and a printed billboard." ‍ Alyona Deieieva, Lead Brand and Marketing Designer at Arounda
When It Makes Sense to Split Into Two Documents
The brand guide vs style guide question comes down to who owns each half and how often each one changes. Here's when a single document stops working and splitting makes sense.

body.alt: When It Makes Sense to Split Into Two Documents
body.caption: When It Makes Sense to Split Into Two Documents

items: **Marketing and design report to different people.** Marketing doesn't touch the design section, and design doesn't touch marketing's. One half gets updated. The other half sits untouched for months.

**Update speed doesn't match.** Logos and colors are not changed often. However, messaging may change every quarter depending on how ad campaigns move. If you add both into one file, every small text edit bumps the "last updated" date on rules that didn't change. People stop trusting that date, and eventually stop checking it before using outdated assets.
**A developer needs the logo file and nothing else.** Making them scroll past ten pages of tone of voice to find a PNG wastes their time and yours.

**Legal or trademark rules apply to one half.** Logo and trademark usage may need legal approval. However, voice and tone rarely do. If you keep them in one document, a five-minute tone of voice edit will wait in the same queue as a trademark review.

**External partners only need one piece.** If a reseller requires logo specs and a guest blogger needs tone guidance, it makes sense to split this into two documents. Sending both the full brand guide means they wade through content meant for someone else.

body.text: When One Combined Document Is the Smarter Choice
The main reasons why having one document is the best decision are as follows:

items: Only one person is responsible for both parts
Teams are small, under 10-15 people
Brand rarely needs legal review
Visual identity guide includes voice
Updates happen together
New employees need to learn the file quickly

body.text: The Brief Template: What to Ask a Design Company For
Here's the brand guidelines checklist, so the company builds the right document on the first try:

items: **The exact document type.** A one-page logo reference and a 50-page voice-and-visual manual both count as "brand guidelines" somewhere. Name which one. What does style guide mean for your team specifically? The design company can't guess that on its own.
**Every audience who’ll open it.** Add internal designers, external partners, developers, freelance writers, etc. Slack's document works for all of them because it names each reader upfront.
**What changes often versus what doesn’t.** Logo and color might stay fixed for five years. Messaging shifts every quarter. This detail decides whether you need one document or two.
**Old materials. **An outdated PDF from 2019 can still tell a designer a lot about your company. So, if you have old materials that can be used for your new brand or style guide, show them.
**Who approves what.** Legal signs off on trademark use. Marketing signs off on tone. Naming this upfront avoids a document with no clear owner for revisions.
**Where the format lives.** Show your PDFs, Notion pages, Figma files, etc. Each one changes how often the document gets updated after launch.
**Every place the brand shows up.** List every surface: web, social, print, partner co-branding, developer docs, app store listings, even[pitch deck design](/services/pitch-deck) for investors.

body.alt: What to Ask a Design Company For
body.caption: What to Ask a Design Company For

body.text: Mistakes We See When Companies Fixate on the Wrong Question

A [2025 report on Kenyan SMEs](https://serrarigroup.com/smes-in-kenya-losing-60-revenue-due-to-poor-branding-new-report-highlights-urgent-need-for-strong-brand-identity/) found poor branding costs businesses up to 60% of potential revenue. Companies spend weeks arguing about the name, then ship a document full of holes. Check out typical mistakes we keep running into:

items: Fighting over "style guide" vs "brand guide" instead of just writing the thing
Grabbing a template that fits a 200-person company when the team has 10
Building something only the design team ever opens
Stuffing it with legal language
Forgetting partners or resellers need their own section
Publishing it once and never touching it again

body.text: Case Study: Building StockGate Brand Documentation

[StockGate](/works/stockgate) turned to Arounda for [branding services](/services/branding) to create a visual identity for its crypto investment platform that would stand out against cold, dark competitor aesthetics and build user trust.

body.alt: StockGate fintech logo and brand identity design
body.caption: StockGate fintech logo and brand identity design

body.text: Our team conducted competitor research and built a human-centered brand system using warm orange, blue, black, and photos of real people. We engineered a geometric logo readable at app-icon scale, in monochrome, and across reversed backgrounds. To support institutional credibility, Arounda documented rules extending the identity across digital social traffic, outdoor ads, business cards, and branded merchandise.
Every branding project delivers a complete brand voice and tone guide covering essential execution rules:

items: Logo specifications, including clear space, app scale, and monochrome variants
Color standards defining primary, accent, and background palettes
Typography hierarchy and visual asset guidelines for photography and 3D elements
Cross-surface guidelines for digital UI, social banners, outdoor print, and physical merchandise

body.text: This documentation provides internal teams and external partners with a single source of truth. Post-launch testing showed 88% of users distinguished StockGate from typical crypto platforms, while 93% reported higher confidence in the platform.
How Arounda Approaches Brand and Style Documentation

The process remains the same for every company, but the level of detail varies by business scale. The thing is that startups need to launch fast, so they are looking for simple guardrails. Larger businesses with multiple products need clear visual rules so everything fits together smoothly.
For SMEs and MVPs
A lightweight starter kit is what startups and small businesses need. It must be a simple guide that outlines primary logo rules, exact color hexes, key fonts, and basic spacing.
For Ecosystems and Corporate Rebranding
Platforms with multiple sub-products deal with higher complexity. The documentation must show how each product keeps its distinct role while clearly fitting under one main brand.

During our [rebranding](/services/rebranding) project for [HRWorkCycles](/works/hrworkcycles), the client managed three HR tools with conflicting visuals that hurt brand awareness. Arounda developed a scalable [brand identity design](/services/brand-identity) around a single geometric framework. Each product received its own logo mark and pattern, while sharing the same color logic and typography. Setting these multi-product guidelines turned three separate tools into one unified system, raising brand recognition by 35% and conversions by 28%.

body.alt: HRWorkCycles brand identity design showing a unified geometric logo system across sub-products.
body.caption: HRWorkCycles brand identity design showing a unified geometric logo system across sub-products.

body.text: "Most brand guides look great at launch, but they break down a few months later. That happens when they only cover ideal scenarios. If you want a guide that lasts, map out everyday edge cases early. Think about dark mode, tiny app icons, or partner co-branding. That is what keeps your brand recognizable long after launch." ‍ Mariia Lysenko, Brand/Marketing Designer at Arounda

Arounda has spent over 10 years building brand systems across 180+ completed projects. That track record shows in a 5.0 rating on [Clutch](https://clutch.co/go-to-review/c00f719f-d36f-4f55-a8aa-b0062884d103/253430). Your brand documentation could be next on that list.
Wrapping Up

We analyzed 15 public brand documents, but the name on each one told us almost nothing about what was inside. Some companies prefer splitting logo rules from voice rules into two files, but others feel more comfortable when everything is kept in one document.

What matters most is whether the visual rules and the reasoning behind them lived in the same place, and whether one person clearly owned each part. However, when different teams are involved, splitting into two documents might be a solution.

title: Mental Health App Design: Principles, Patterns, and What Works
author: Valeriia Serohina
excerpt: Nearly 1.2 billion people worldwide had a mental disorder,[almost double the number from 1990](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/05/21/health/mental-disorder-rate-worldwide-study-wellness). Anxiety and depression were the main reasons for that g

body.text: Nearly 1.2 billion people worldwide had a mental disorder,[almost double the number from 1990](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/05/21/health/mental-disorder-rate-worldwide-study-wellness). Anxiety and depression were the main reasons for that growth. If you're building a wellness app right now, some of your users already carry one of these diagnoses.

Mental health app design carries a weight most software never has to carry. A confusing screen in a banking app costs a user a few minutes, but the same screen during a panic attack can cost someone the one moment they reached out for help.

[Arounda](/) has been designing mental health apps for over 10 years, and this guide comes from that experience. It covers the patterns that hold up under emotional strain and the mistakes that quietly push users away. In this article, our designers show case studies that demonstrate what changes when the interface gets it right.
Article Key Takeaways

items: Mental health apps have much higher stakes than most software. Users download such apps with reduced capacity, and that is why an overloaded screen can cost someone their one shot at getting help that day.
Trust, speed to the right action, and consistency are more important than the number of features added or a polished look.
Fixed navigation, one clear action instead of a menu, an always-visible crisis button, and progress tracking that doesn't punish setbacks make the biggest difference.
Our real cases like [Lyynk](/works/lyynk), [Cognify](/works/cognify), and [Lumera](/works/lumera) show these ideas in practice, with commentary from Arounda's design team on what holds up.

body.text: Why Mental Health App Design Is Different

A confusing checkout flow costs an e-commerce app a sale. A confusing mental health app costs a person their only attempt to get support that day. Here are the main criteria that differentiate mental health apps from other consumer software products:

items: **Users arrive with less capacity.** Anxiety, depression, and stress make it harder to think clearly. People can't make decisions quickly. Someone in the middle of a panic attack isn't going to figure out a five-tab menu. Every extra step takes effort and makes them close the app and never open it again.

**The stakes of a bad interaction are higher.** Poor usability is the top reason people stop using mental health apps, according to an analysis of [over 13,000 App Store and Google Play reviews](https://www.jmir.org/2024/1/e56897). A person who abandons one app after a bad experience often doesn't try another.

body.alt: Why Mental Health App Design Is Different
body.caption: Why Mental Health App Design Is Different

body.text: We have some retention numbers that prove this. Median 30-day retention for mental health apps is around 3.3%, and a scoping review found a[median of 70% of users quit within 100 days](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11694054/). Most of that drop-off happens because of the friction in the interface.
Here's what this means for the design:

items: **Trust has to come before anything else.** Someone opening a mental health app is often about to type things they haven't said out loud to anyone. If the first screen feels like a form at a doctor's office (all boxes and fine print), they hesitate or just close the app. Explaining why you need a mood check-in, or letting someone skip a question, builds more trust than any privacy badge.

**Speed to the thing that helps matters more than how many features you built.** People suffering from mental health illnesses don't want to land on a dashboard with mood graphs and 3-4 suggested articles. They want the breathing exercise or crisis line right there.
**Consistency outweighs novelty.** A layout that shifts between sessions adds cognitive load when the user has the least of it to spare.

body.text: Design here is of utmost importance, as it shows if the app was built for a user whose state determines whether the product works at all.
Case Study: Designing Lyynk

[Lyynk](/works/lyynk) is a French platform where young people can track their emotions and stay in touch with an adult they trust. The product was a bit messy; it had too many features stacked on top of each other, a maze of navigation, and an outdated look. However, teens needed something soft and much easier to use. The adults on the other side needed something they could rely on. GDPR rules for underage users added a third layer to design around. Arounda took it through a full[UI/UX design](/services/ui-ux-design) process, starting with a[UX audit](/services/ux-audit) of the existing app, then rebuilding the visual identity with[graphic design](/services/graphic-design) work.

body.alt: Lyynk: Healthcare mobile app redesign | Arounda case
body.caption: Lyynk: Healthcare mobile app redesign | Arounda case

body.text: What was changed by our expert team:

items: Stripped the app down to the features people use every single day
Rebuilt mood tracking, journaling, and shared activities
Fixed the crisis button in one place and made it more visible
Shifted the visual system to muted colors and soft 3D icons that read as calm

body.text: Results after launch:

items: 100k+ downloads
4.8★ app store rating
+38% growth in engagement
+42% increase in retention

body.text: That last figure matters most. Most mental health apps lose the majority of their users in the first 30 days (often before the app has a chance to help anyone). Lyynk moved 42% in the opposite direction after the redesign. So people who downloaded it kept coming back again and again.
Mistakes We Keep Seeing in Mental Health App Design

Most of these mistakes come from teams optimizing for the wrong thing. They chase a polished look, a longer feature list, or a friendlier onboarding flow, but as a result, they add more steps that a distressed user doesn't have the patience for. A simple [UX audit](/services/ux-audit) can catch these issues quickly. See the table below that covers all typical mistakes and offers ways to solve them.
The pattern across all of these is the same. Every mistake in mental health app UI design adds a step between someone feeling bad and getting help, so fixing them means cutting those steps.
Core UI/UX Patterns for Mental Health Apps

Look at almost any mental health app people stick with, and the same five mental wellness app design patterns show up. They all mean putting the user's state ahead of the usual design instincts, even when that goes against what looks impressive in a portfolio. Here are the main design patterns.
Navigation That Never Moves

Under stress conditions, people rely more on muscle memory. Therefore, the best solution is to keep the same menu in the same spots across every version and every update. Calm and Headspace both kept a fixed bottom tab bar for years for this reason. As a result, a returning user never has to relearn where anything lives.
**Arounda suggests:** don't redesign navigation during a rebrand. You can change colors or icons (if you want to), but it is better not to touch tab positions and the main structure.
One Clear Action, Not a Menu
A home screen with 5-7 buttons forces a decision nobody in crisis wants to make. There are basically two ways to design this:

items: **Menu-first:** a grid of features, and the user has to guess which one helps right now
**Action-first:** one clear prompt front and center, everything else just one tap away

body.text: People dealing with insomnia or depression need to take supplements or medication at the right time every day. Arounda ran into this while designing[Luma](/works/luma), a healthcare app for supplement routines. The team pulled out the usual dashboard and replaced it with a single daily plan: one recommended action. Retention doubled after the change, and 7-day plan adherence climbed to 64%.
A Way to Exit Without Guilt

Avoid using too pushy pop-ups like this one – "Are you sure you want to give up?" If someone starts a breathing exercise or a journal entry and changes their mind halfway through, closing the application should take one tap only.
**Arounda suggests:** save confirmation dialogs for things that are hard to undo (deleting a journal entry or an account). For everything else, let people leave. No guilt trip on the way out.
Progress That Doesn't Punish Setbacks

Streaks are a powerful tool for fitness mobile apps, but here, they backfire. The thing is that in this context, a missed day can mean that a user was struggling (it is not a case of skipping out). That is why resetting a counter to zero can punish the person who needs the app the most.

When Arounda redesigned[Lyynk](/works/lyynk), the team skipped the streak counter entirely. Mood tracking and journaling were built around each user's own rhythm, with a personalized review flow that adapts to how someone journals and doesn't punish gaps.

body.alt: Lyynk: Progress visualization for a healthcare app | Arounda case
body.caption: Lyynk: Progress visualization for a healthcare app | Arounda case

body.text: A Crisis Button Users Can Always Find

A crisis button is one of the key features here, and it must be placed in the same corner of every screen. Don't hide it in a hamburger menu or settings. Top crisis-line apps anchor this in the navigation bar itself, so it always stays visible for people under pressure.

For[Lyynk](/works/lyynk), placing crisis support where teens could find it fast, without making the whole app feel like a clinical intervention tool, was one of the harder design problems the team solved. It had to stay visible enough to use in a real crisis.

**Arounda suggests:** treat the crisis button placement as a rule (it is not a design choice open for iteration). Every new screen must be tested against the question of “can people under stress find it within a few seconds or not?”
Visual and Interaction Design Principles
Colors and motion change how someone's nervous system reacts to the screen, sometimes within the first second of opening the app.
Color and Typography for Calm

Saturated colors and high contrast read as urgent, which is the opposite of what someone dealing with anxiety needs. Most digital therapeutics design choices rely on muted, low-saturation palettes: soft blues, sage greens, dusty lavender. For example, Calm's interface stays almost entirely desaturated, and Headspace pairs its brighter accents with large amounts of white space. As a result, nothing feels too loud.

"Honestly, most of what we do is take stuff away. A color here, an animation there. Someone opening this app might already be overwhelmed, so every extra thing on the screen is one more thing fighting for their attention. ‍ ‍ Valeriia Serohina | Art Director at Arounda

A[2026 scoping review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13437323/) of 16 studies and over 4,000 participants found that people with depressive and anxiety-related disorders consistently gravitated toward blue, grey, and darker shades. Participants without a diagnosis almost never picked black, grey, or white as a favorite color. That shows what people in a low mood state prefer, which is still a reason to think twice before defaulting to the loud palettes that work fine for a shopping app.

Typography is also of utmost importance. Rounded sans-serif fonts read as friendlier than sharp, geometric ones, and text needs room to breathe since anxious readers scan faster and skip words when lines sit too tight.
**Arounda suggests: **here’s what needs to be avoided:

items: Bright red for anything other than a genuine crisis alert
Low-contrast gray text on white backgrounds
All-caps buttons, which read as aggressive

body.text: Motion, Haptics, and Sensory Neutrality
Animation should confirm that something happened. So the best solution is to keep transitions short, under 300 milliseconds, and let them fade or slide.
Haptic feedback needs the same restraint. A single soft tap on completing an exercise feels supportive. A pattern of buzzes on every tap starts to feel like nagging.

This matters even more in a crisis intervention UI. Someone reaching for a panic button doesn't need an animated transition between their tap and the help on the other side. The best crisis flows skip decorative motion entirely: one tap, then the resource appears. Every extra half-second is too long.
Sounds should also be calm and relaxing. The thing is that an unexpected chime can be jarring for someone using the app in public or during a moment they'd rather keep private.
What Compliance Changes in the Interface

Compliance decides what shows up on screen, what stays hidden, and how fast certain things have to disappear. Every project Arounda takes on in this space gets designed around these rules from the first wireframe. A rule written in a legal document like GDPR or [HIPAA](/blog/hipaa-compliant-website-design)turns into a consent screen, a lock timer, a permission setting, something a designer has to draw and place.

items: **Consent screens come first. **Before a journal entry saves anything a user types, GDPR and HIPAA both say the app needs clear permission first. That can be a short screen that shows up right when someone opens a mood check-in for the first time. It must be easy to read and explain what's being saved and for what reasons.
**Sessions lock themselves.** Auto-lock after inactivity and screens that clear sensitive text when the app goes to the background exist because someone else could pick up the phone at any moment.

**Access gets split by role.** Apps built for kids or young people require separate permission levels. As a result, a parent can always stay involved. A good mental wellness app UI design makes that boundary visible to both sides.

**Crisis messages trigger a response.** If someone types something like "I don't want to be here anymore," the interface has to respond in that moment, whether that's a hotline number or a direct line to a trusted contact.

**Deleting your data has to be easy to find.** Users have a legal right to export or delete what they've shared. That means a button for it. In this case, a support email hidden in the FAQ won’t help.

body.text: All five of these are also cognitive accessibility design choices. Clear consent, predictable locking, visible boundaries, and an easy way out all reduce the mental effort it takes to use the app safely.
Why Good Design Work Pays Off in Retention and Funding
Design decisions can directly influence how many users will download the app and get the most out of it.

Retention comes down to one thing: does the app still work for someone on their worst day, three weeks in? A crisis button that's always in the same spot, adaptive UI mental health screens that don't shuffle around between visits, and a therapy app design that gets someone to a breathing exercise or a chat in one tap instead of hunting through five, all of that adds up to someone opening the app again next week instead of deleting it.
Lyynk is proof this isn't theoretical. This app was rebuilt around exactly these ideas, and retention went up 42%.

Funding follows a similar logic. Investors evaluating a mental health app always pay attention to how the app works. A 4.8★ rating and steady user growth carry more weight in a pitch deck than a polished mockup.

Weak design tends to surface during due diligence as low retention or unresolved compliance gaps, and that's a harder story to tell investors. That's why many early-stage teams get[startup web design](/services/startup-web-design-agency) help before they start pitching, so the product backs up the story they're telling. Good design earns its place in both a growth chart and a term sheet.

"When my team designs, we keep an eye on the stuff a product owner watches: retention, drop-off, time to value, conversion. But we also think about risk, because that's what investors care about. Low churn, steady engagement, no compliance mess, that's what makes a product feel safer to put money into." ‍ ‍ Vlad Gavriluk , Founder and CEO at Arounda
UI Design Examples Worth Studying
Here's how three products used Arounda's[UI/UX design services](/services/ui-ux-design) to put these mental health app UI design patterns into practice, with the numbers to back it up.
Lumera: Mental Wellness Platform (UI/UX Design)

[Lumera](/works/lumera) is an AI-powered mental wellness app. It was built for users already drowning in digital noise. The biggest challenge here was to turn too complex mood analytics into something that felt like a reflection. Arounda's team stripped the interface down to one idea per screen and dropped the typical dashboard grid. On top of that, designers built the UI around an editorial reading rhythm.

items: Trial signups up 34%
CTA click rate up 27%
Bounce rate down 22%
Feature discovery up 36%

body.text: Simplifying an information-heavy mental wellness app design makes people trust it enough to explore further.
Cognify: Cognitive Health Platform (Web App Design)

[Cognify](/works/cognify) tracks biometric signals for knowledge workers and warns them when stress is building, before it turns into full-on burnout. The tricky part was the data itself. Raw biometric charts are full of numbers nobody wants to decode between meetings. Users needed to glance at the screen and just know what to do next.

Here's what the Arounda team did. Instead of throwing all the data at users right away, the dashboard leads with a clear answer: your status right now and what to do about it. If someone wants to find out more about stress trends, scan results, or biomarker details, that's all there too, just one layer down. It doesn't crowd the main screen.

[Mine'd](https://arounda.agency/case/mined) is a relationship and emotional wellness platform. It serves two separate audiences from one product: people seeking guidance and the experts providing it. Results:

8% conversion rate

body.text: Building two separate flows, one for each audience, is what made both sides of the platform work well together.
How Arounda Approaches Mental Health App Design

Every project starts with the same question: what does this person need in the moment they're most likely to give up? A [full redesign](/services/website-redesign) or [MVP development](/services/mvp-development) – all other steps are organized around the answer to this question:

items: **Map emotions before screens.** Before drawing a single wireframe, the team needs to map out the emotional states users go through. And this map becomes the backbone of the whole design flow. Simply put, the navigation follows how someone feels instead of a generic structure borrowed from a to-do list or a shopping app.

**Keeping one idea per screen.** We avoid using a dashboard that stacks five things at once. Each screen must carry a single focus, so reflection doesn't turn into information overload, and Lumera is a good example.

**Leading with the answer.** Show the status and the recommendation first, then let deeper data sit one layer down for anyone who wants to dig in. Cognify's dashboard works this way. It opens with a clear read on the user's state before any of the underlying numbers.

**Design for every role separately.** Mine'd needed two distinct experiences for two different users: consumers and experts, so Arounda built separate flows that didn’t force one layout to serve both.
**Building compliance from day one.** GDPR requirements for Lyynk's teenage users shaped permission levels and privacy controls from the first wireframe, not as a patch after launch.
